drugRefs.regimenLabel: Penicillin V (oral) or Penicillin G (IV if systemic symptoms)
drugRefs.dose: Penicillin V 500 mg PO q6h or Penicillin G 2-4 million units IV q6h
drugRefs.route: Oral or IV depending on severity
drugRefs.why: Penicillin remains first-line given the near-universal streptococcal etiology of erysipelas - a narrow-spectrum choice is appropriate and avoids unnecessary staphylococcal coverage needed for true cellulitis.

refs: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

drugRefs.coverage: Alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients, retaining reliable streptococcal coverage.

refs: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

coverageMatrix.completeness: Penicillin provides essentially complete coverage of the expected pathogens in classic erysipelas.
gaps: If atypical features (purulence, abscess) are present, reconsider the diagnosis toward cellulitis/abscess with staphylococcal coverage rather than treating as erysipelas.

stewardship.deescalation: Not typically needed given the reliably narrow-spectrum, targeted first-line therapy; reassess if not improving within 48-72 hours, which should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.

framework: Avoid broader-spectrum staphylococcal coverage by default - the sharply demarcated border is a genuinely useful clinical sign supporting narrow-spectrum penicillin therapy.
Elevate the affected limb and manage predisposing factors (lymphedema, venous insufficiency, tinea pedis as an entry point) to reduce recurrence risk.
Recurrent erysipelas may warrant prophylactic antibiotics in consultation with a specialist - this is a separate long-term decision from acute treatment.
